newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon says Ericsson misinterprets $147 mln deal.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon says Ericsson misinterprets $147 mln deal.

text.p: Lebanon said on Thursday it was involved in a $70 million dollars disagreement with Swedish telecoms giant LM Ericsson over a contract to install thousands of new telephone lines in Lebanon.
A telecommunications official told Reuters the disagreement was due to Ericsson's misinterpretation of the contract.

Ghassan Assi, Director General of Equipment and Construction at the Ministry of Posts and Telecommunications said the March 1994 contract was for the provision of 225,000 switched lines at a cost of $147 million.
"Their (Ericsson's) understanding of what the contract includes is different from ours. It's about $70 million different from our understanding," Assi said.
He said Ericsson expected an additional $70 million payment for work that it considered outside the contract.
"We are still trying to sort out the differences amicably and have not reached the point of no return," Assi said.

A report on Monday in the Swedish daily Dagens Industri said the Lebanese telecoms authority had asserted that Ericsson carried out work worth $147 million as stated in the contract but then did more work, using its own resources.

The report said Ericsson said Lebanese authorities had asked for more than was stated in the contract and therefore owed the company more. It said the contract was for 170,000 telephone lines, while Assi said it was for 225,000 switched lines.
Asked to comment on the report, Assi said Lebanon had not asked Ericsson to do any extra work.
"We have not asked them to carry out any work additional to the contract and they haven't executed any such work, far from it," he said.

"We never asserted that Ericsson carried out work worth $147 million. So far they have executed one third of the contract. They are 20 percent late on project implementation and still far from achieving their targets and far from invoicing against the $147 million," he added.
The March 1994 deal included provision of buildings, lines, boxes, cabinets, trenches and poles, Assi said. He declined to specify further the points of difference.
Dagens Industri said the situation between Ericsson and the Lebanese authorities was critical and there was a risk that the dispute would have to go to arbitration.
Assi said it was up to Ericsson to decide whether to seek arbitration, which he called a complicated and time-consuming process.

"We will not seek arbitration," he said. "But if the situation gets to that stage then we are ready for it and we are confident with our position because the contract is very clear and it was interpreted by numerous international legal authorities.
"It is to the disadvantage of Ericsson to decide to stop work because if they do so they will very well be in breach of the contract. I don't think they want that," he added.
Assi said Lebanese authorities were amicably sorting out similar differences with the French and German telecoms companies Alcatel and Siemens.
"I can confidently say that by the end of September we will have resolved all our differences with Alcatel and Siemens," Assi said.
The telecommunication ministry signed deals with Alcatel and Siemens in March 1994 worth $130 million and $153 million for the provision of 225,000 lines and 350,000 lines respectively.
